sectionTitle: Hazards and uses of radioactive emissions and of background radiation (physics only)

specStatements.text: Background radiation is around us all of the time. It comes from:
• natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays from space
• man-made sources such as the fallout from nuclear weapons testing and nuclear accidents.
The level of background radiation and radiation dose may be affected by occupation and/or location.
Radiation dose is measured in sieverts (Sv)
Students will not need to recall the unit of radiation dose.
Radioactive isotopes have a very wide range of half-life values.
Students should be able to explain why the hazards associated with radioactive material differ according to the half-life involved.
Nuclear radiations are used in medicine for the:
• control or destruction of unwanted tissue.
• describe and evaluate the uses of nuclear radiations for exploration of internal organs, and for control or destruction of unwanted tissue
• evaluate the perceived risks of using nuclear radiations in relation to given data and consequences.

scopeNotes.statement: Students will not need to recall the unit of radiation dose.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item in this section asks a student to name, recall or select the unit of radiation dose from memory. Every item that involves dose supplies the unit inside the stem — 'a radiation dose of 4.5 mSv', 'a dose of 2500 mSv', 'Using 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv)' — and then asks the student to interpret what the value means, to convert between the two units given, or to weigh one supplied dose against another. The sievert and the millisievert are defined in c09 and c10 as supporting information, so that data presented in an examination can be read with understanding, never as a fact to be reproduced unprompted.

concepts.definition: The low-level ionising radiation that is around us all of the time. It comes from natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays from space, and from man-made sources such as the fallout from nuclear weapons testing and nuclear accidents.

Sources that are not the result of human activity, such as rocks and cosmic rays from space. Rocks in the ground and in building materials contain radioactive isotopes, so some radiation is always present.

Ionising radiation that arrives at the Earth from space. The atmosphere absorbs much of it, so the dose from cosmic rays is greater at high altitude than at sea level. Cosmic rays are a natural source of background radiation.
Sources that are present because of human activity, such as the fallout from nuclear weapons testing and from nuclear accidents. They add to the natural background rather than replacing it.

Radioactive material thrown into the atmosphere by nuclear weapons testing or by a nuclear accident, which then settles onto the ground and onto vegetation over a wide area. Fallout is a man-made source of background radiation.

concepts.term: Effect of occupation on radiation dose
concepts.definition: Some jobs bring extra exposure to radiation, so the dose a person receives depends partly on their occupation. Radiographers, nuclear industry workers and aircrew, for example, receive higher annual doses than most other workers.

concepts.term: Effect of location on radiation dose
concepts.definition: The level of background radiation varies from place to place, so dose depends partly on where a person lives or travels. Ground and buildings of granite release more radon gas, and exposure to cosmic rays rises with altitude.
A measure of the risk of harm to body tissue as a result of exposure to ionising radiation. It depends on both the amount of radiation absorbed and the type of radiation the body has been exposed to.
The unit in which radiation dose is measured. A dose stated in sieverts describes the risk to the body, not how radioactive a source is; the activity of a source is measured separately in becquerels.
A smaller unit of radiation dose, used because everyday doses are far below one sievert. 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), so a dose given in mSv is divided by 1000 to convert it into Sv.
Radioactive isotopes have a very wide range of half-life values, from small fractions of a second for some isotopes to many thousands of millions of years for others.

The hazard from a radioactive material depends on its half-life. A short half-life means a high activity that falls away quickly, so the material is intensely radioactive at first but soon becomes much safer. A long half-life means a lower activity that persists, so the material stays hazardous for a very long time.
Nuclear radiations are used in medicine for the exploration of internal organs and for the control or destruction of unwanted tissue.

A substance containing a radioactive isotope that is taken into the body so that an internal organ can be explored. A gamma emitter with a short half-life is used, because gamma radiation passes out of the body to a detector and the activity soon falls away.

The use of nuclear radiation to control or destroy unwanted tissue such as a tumour. A high dose of gamma radiation is directed at the tumour from outside the body, or an implanted source is placed so that the dose is concentrated where it is needed.

The risk people believe a nuclear radiation carries is often different from the risk shown by data. Evaluating a medical use means comparing the dose received, and its consequences, with the benefit of the diagnosis or treatment and with the risk of doing nothing.

misconceptions.question: If there has been no nuclear accident near you, is there any radiation around you now?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Background radiation is around us all of the time.
misconceptions.misconception: There is normally no radiation around us; it only appears in a place after an accident or a leak.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Radiation is reported in the news almost only in connection with accidents and weapons, so students tie its presence to disaster rather than to ordinary life.
misconceptions.correction: Background radiation is present continuously and everywhere. It comes from natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays from space as well as from man-made sources. An accident raises the level in a place; it does not create radiation where there was none.

misconceptions.question: Fallout contains atoms of elements that also occur in nature. Does that make it a natural source?
misconceptions.correct: No. Fallout from nuclear weapons testing and from nuclear accidents is a man-made source.
misconceptions.misconception: Fallout counts as a natural source, because the radioactive atoms in it are the same kinds of atom that are found in rocks.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students classify a source by what the material is made of rather than by how it came to be there, and once fallout has settled into soil it looks like part of the ground.
misconceptions.correction: Sources are classified by origin. Fallout is in the environment because people tested weapons or because a reactor failed, so it is man-made, however ordinary the atoms in it may be.

misconceptions.question: Does background radiation exist only because people have built reactors and weapons?
misconceptions.correct: No. Much of the background comes from natural sources that were there long before any nuclear technology.
misconceptions.misconception: All background radiation is left over from human nuclear activity, so without reactors and weapons there would be none at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The man-made sources are the ones with memorable names and stories attached, so they dominate a student's picture of where radiation comes from.
misconceptions.correction: Rocks and cosmic rays from space are natural sources and have always contributed. Man-made sources such as fallout add to this natural background; they are not the whole of it.

misconceptions.question: Are cosmic rays simply a part of ordinary sunlight?
misconceptions.correct: No. Cosmic rays are ionising radiation arriving from space, and they reach us by night as well as by day.
misconceptions.misconception: Cosmic rays are just sunlight, so you only receive them outdoors on a sunny day.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The only radiation from space that students meet daily is sunlight, so 'from space' is read as 'from the Sun', and the word rays reinforces it.
misconceptions.correction: Cosmic rays are high-energy ionising radiation from space that reaches the Earth all of the time. The atmosphere absorbs much of it, which is why the dose is larger at high altitude.

misconceptions.question: Is background radiation the same everywhere, so that everybody receives the same dose?
misconceptions.correct: No. The level of background radiation and radiation dose may be affected by occupation and/or location.
misconceptions.misconception: Background radiation is a fixed amount, identical for everybody, so no one person's dose can be higher than anybody else's.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word background suggests a constant baseline, and textbook figures are often quoted as a single average value with no range given.
misconceptions.correction: The level varies. Living where the rock is granite, or at high altitude, raises the dose from natural sources, and some occupations bring extra exposure on top of that.

misconceptions.question: Aircrew are far above the rocks in the ground. Does that mean they receive a smaller dose?
misconceptions.correct: No. At altitude there is less atmosphere above you to absorb cosmic rays, so the dose is larger.
misconceptions.misconception: Height puts you further from the radioactive rocks, so background radiation must fall as you go up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember one natural source, the ground, and reason only about distance from it, forgetting that cosmic rays arrive from the other direction.
misconceptions.correction: Two natural sources act in opposite directions with height. The contribution from rock falls, but the cosmic ray contribution rises much more because less air shields you, so the total dose goes up.

misconceptions.question: Does a radiation dose in sieverts tell you how much radioactive material a person contains?
misconceptions.correct: No. Dose is a measure of the risk of harm to the body from the radiation it has absorbed.
misconceptions.misconception: A dose is like a dose of medicine: it is the quantity of radioactive substance given to the patient.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In every other context a dose is an amount of a substance, so students carry that meaning across without questioning it.
misconceptions.correction: Radiation dose measures the effect on the body, not an amount of material. It depends on how much radiation was absorbed and on the type of radiation, and it is measured in sieverts.

misconceptions.question: Do sieverts and becquerels measure the same thing?
misconceptions.correct: No. Activity in becquerels describes the source; dose in sieverts describes the risk to the person exposed.
misconceptions.misconception: Both units say how radioactive something is, so a dose figure can be read as a count of decays.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both units appear in the same topic and both get larger when there is more radiation, so students merge them into one idea.
misconceptions.correction: Activity counts decays per second in a source. Dose measures the harm risked by a body that absorbs radiation, and two people beside the same source can receive very different doses.

misconceptions.question: To change a dose in millisieverts into sieverts, do you multiply by 1000?
misconceptions.correct: No. 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), so a value in mSv is divided by 1000 to give sieverts.
misconceptions.misconception: Converting units always means multiplying by the number in the relationship, whichever way the conversion goes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn conversions as 'find the number and multiply' without deciding first whether the answer should come out larger or smaller than the value they started with.
misconceptions.correction: Check the size of the answer. A millisievert is smaller than a sievert, so a dose in mSv must give a smaller number when written in Sv: divide by 1000.

misconceptions.question: Are half-lives all roughly the same size, a few years or so?
misconceptions.correct: No. Radioactive isotopes have a very wide range of half-life values.
misconceptions.misconception: Half-lives all fall into a narrow band, because the examples used in class are of a similar size.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Practice questions use convenient half-lives of minutes, days or years so that graphs fit on a page, so the extremes are never seen.
misconceptions.correction: The range is enormous, from small fractions of a second to thousands of millions of years, and that range is what makes some isotopes suitable as tracers and others a long-term waste problem.

misconceptions.question: Does a long half-life mean a material is more dangerous at this moment?
misconceptions.correct: No. A long half-life means a low activity that lasts, so the hazard is that the material stays radioactive for a very long time.
misconceptions.misconception: Long half-life means more radioactive, so such a material must be giving out radiation intensely right now.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Long is read as more, and the long-lived isotopes in nuclear waste are the ones talked about as dangerous, so the two ideas fuse.
misconceptions.correction: For a given number of atoms, a long half-life means decays are rare, so the activity is low. The danger is duration: the material remains a hazard long after it has been spilled or buried.

misconceptions.question: Is a source with a half-life of a few minutes harmless?
misconceptions.correct: No. Its activity is very high while it lasts, so it is a serious hazard at first even though it soon decays away.
misconceptions.misconception: A short half-life means the material has essentially gone, so it can be treated as safe from the start.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that short-lived tracers are chosen to protect patients and conclude that short half-life is simply a synonym for safe.
misconceptions.correction: A short half-life means many decays each second at the beginning, so the immediate hazard is large. It becomes safe later, not now, and that is exactly why it must be handled carefully at first.

misconceptions.question: Would an alpha emitter make the best tracer for exploring an internal organ?
misconceptions.correct: No. A gamma emitter is used, because gamma radiation passes out of the body and can be detected outside.
misconceptions.misconception: The most strongly ionising radiation must give the clearest picture, so alpha is the best choice for a scan.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate strong ionisation with a strong signal, and they do not check whether the radiation can escape the body to reach a detector at all.
misconceptions.correction: Alpha is stopped by a sheet of paper, by the skin or by a few centimetres of air, so it travels less than a millimetre into tissue. Nothing reaches the detector and all of the ionisation is deposited in the patient. Gamma is weakly ionising and penetrating, which is what a tracer needs.

misconceptions.question: In radiotherapy, is healthy tissue completely unaffected because the beam is aimed at the tumour?
misconceptions.correct: No. Tissue in the path of the beam also receives a dose, which is why the treatment has side effects.
misconceptions.misconception: Targeting means that only the tumour receives radiation, so radiotherapy carries no risk to the rest of the body.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word targeted, and diagrams showing a single arrow striking a tumour, suggest that the radiation begins and ends at the target.
misconceptions.correction: The beam must pass through healthy tissue to reach a tumour inside the body. Rotating the beam around the patient keeps the tumour in the path while spreading the dose to healthy tissue over a larger volume.

misconceptions.question: If a scan gives a dose above the natural background, should it always be refused?
misconceptions.correct: No. The extra risk from the dose has to be weighed against the medical benefit and the consequences of not being scanned.
misconceptions.misconception: Any exposure to nuclear radiation is unacceptable, so no medical dose can ever be justified.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Radiation is presented in public discussion as uniquely dangerous, and students have no everyday scale on which to judge one dose figure against another.
misconceptions.correction: Risk is a matter of degree. A dose of a few millisieverts raises the chance of harm only slightly, while an undiagnosed or untreated illness may be far more dangerous, so given data must be compared, not simply rejected.

misconceptions.question: Does a patient given a radioactive tracer stay radioactive permanently?
misconceptions.correct: No. The activity falls as the isotope decays, and a short half-life is chosen so that it falls quickly.
misconceptions.misconception: Once a radioactive substance is inside you, you remain radioactive for the rest of your life.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think of the substance as contamination that cannot be removed, and they do not connect that idea to the decay curve they have drawn in another lesson.
misconceptions.correction: The nuclei decay, so the activity falls. A tracer with a half-life of a few hours has almost no activity left after a day, and it is also gradually excreted from the body.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about background radiation is correct?

options.text: It is around us all of the time, from natural and from man-made sources.
options.rationale: Background radiation is continuously present, and it has both natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays from space and man-made sources such as fallout.

options.text: It is present only in an area that a nuclear accident has affected.
options.rationale: Radiation is reported in the news mainly when something goes wrong, so students tie its presence to accidents rather than to ordinary surroundings.

options.text: It exists only because people have built reactors and weapons.
options.rationale: The man-made sources are the memorable ones, so the whole background is assumed to be left over from human nuclear activity.

options.text: It is found only in places where uranium-bearing rock lies.
options.rationale: A student who has learned that rocks are a source over-restricts it to ore-bearing ground and forgets cosmic rays and man-made sources.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a natural source of background radiation?

options.text: Fallout still present from earlier nuclear weapons tests
options.rationale: Fallout has settled into the soil and looks like part of the ground, so students classify it by what it is rather than by how it got there.

options.text: Cosmic rays that reach the Earth's surface from space
options.rationale: Cosmic rays from space are named in the specification as a natural source of background radiation, alongside rocks.

options.text: Radioactive waste kept in a store at a power plant
options.rationale: Stored waste is a real source of radiation, but it is present because of human activity, so it is man-made rather than natural.

options.text: Radiation produced by an X-ray machine in a hospital
options.rationale: Students who treat every source of radiation as equivalent overlook that this one is switched on by people and so is not natural.

mcqs.stem: An accident at a nuclear power station releases radioactive material that settles over nearby farmland. How should this contribution to the background radiation there be classified?

options.text: As natural, because the isotopes also occur in rocks
options.rationale: Classifying by the identity of the atoms rather than by their origin is the commonest error made with fallout.

options.text: As natural, since the fallout now lies in soil
options.rationale: Once material is in the ground it feels like part of the landscape, so students reassign it to the natural category.

options.text: As man-made, because human activity released it
options.rationale: The specification lists the fallout from nuclear accidents as a man-made source; the classification depends on origin, not on where the material ends up.

options.text: As neither, because the material has spread widely
options.rationale: Dilution reduces the level but does not change what kind of source it is, a distinction students blur when a source is spread thin.

mcqs.stem: Which pair are both man-made sources of background radiation?

options.text: Cosmic rays from space and rocks lying in the earth
options.rationale: A student who believes all background radiation comes from human activity reads the two natural sources as man-made ones.

options.text: Rocks in the ground and waste from nuclear accidents
options.rationale: This pair mixes one natural and one man-made source, and is chosen by students who class rock-borne radiation as human in origin.

options.text: Cosmic rays from space and fallout from weapons tests
options.rationale: Cosmic rays sound technological to students who think of them as something produced rather than as radiation arriving from space.

options.text: Fallout from weapons testing and nuclear accidents
options.rationale: These are exactly the two man-made sources named in the specification.

mcqs.stem: A radiographer in a hospital records a higher annual radiation dose than an office worker who lives in the same street. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Everyone receives the same dose, so the readings must be faulty.
options.rationale: Students who treat background radiation as one fixed figure for everybody conclude that a difference in dose cannot be real.

options.text: Her occupation exposes her to radiation that the office worker never meets.
options.rationale: The specification states that radiation dose may be affected by occupation; work with X-ray equipment and radioactive sources adds to her dose.

options.text: Radiation collects in the body of anybody who works indoors all day.
options.rationale: The idea that exposure accumulates permanently inside a person is a widespread confusion between being irradiated and staying radioactive.

options.text: Hospitals stand on ground whose rock gives out much more radiation.
options.rationale: This substitutes the location factor for the occupation factor, using a plausible-sounding but invented feature of hospital sites.

mcqs.stem: People living where the local rock is granite, and aircrew who fly long-haul routes, both receive above-average annual radiation doses. Which statement explains both cases?

options.text: Fallout from nuclear weapons tests gathers on high ground and on granite.
options.rationale: Reaching for a man-made source is common when a student cannot see how one natural explanation covers two different situations.

options.text: Both groups spend much more of their working time above sea level.
options.rationale: Height is the only variable the student notices, and it does not in fact apply to people living on granite at low altitude.

options.text: Location affects dose: granite gives radon, altitude gives cosmic rays.
options.rationale: The specification states that the level of background radiation may be affected by location; radon from rock and cosmic rays are both natural sources whose level varies with where you are.

options.text: Dose depends only on occupation, so both groups must share a job.
options.rationale: Students who have learned one factor apply it everywhere, ignoring that the specification names location as well as occupation.

mcqs.stem: A safety leaflet states that a worker received a radiation dose of 4.5 mSv during one year. What does this dose value describe?

options.text: The number of counts that her detector recorded each second.
options.rationale: Activity and dose are met together and both rise when there is more radiation, so students read a dose figure as a count rate.

options.text: The number of nuclei that decayed in the sources she used.
options.rationale: This describes the activity of the source rather than the effect on the person, the other half of the same confusion.

options.text: The mass of radioactive material she took into her body.
options.rationale: In every other context a dose is a quantity of a substance, so students transfer that meaning to radiation dose.

options.text: The risk of harm to her body from the radiation absorbed.
options.rationale: Radiation dose measures the risk of harm to body tissue from the radiation absorbed; it depends on the amount and the type of radiation.

mcqs.stem: A patient's total radiation dose over a course of treatment is 2500 mSv. Using 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), what is this dose in sieverts?

options.text: 2.5 Sv
options.rationale: A millisievert is one thousandth of a sievert, so 2500 mSv is divided by 1000, giving 2.5 Sv.
Dividing by 1000 twice gives this value, which is a thousand times too small; the student converts once too often.
Multiplying by 1000 instead of dividing is the standard conversion error when the direction of the conversion is not checked.
Leaving the number unchanged treats the millisievert and the sievert as though they were the same size of unit.

mcqs.stem: A worker's badge records a dose of 45 mSv over one year. Using 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), what is this dose in sieverts?

options.text: 45 Sv
options.rationale: Copying the number across without converting treats a millisievert as though it were the same size as a sievert.

options.text: 4.5 Sv
options.rationale: Dividing by 10 rather than by 1000 comes from remembering that milli means small without recalling the factor.
45 mSv divided by 1000 gives 0.045 Sv, correctly a smaller number than the value in millisieverts.
Dividing by 100 instead of 1000 is a frequent slip when the prefix milli is treated as a hundredth.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the half-life values of radioactive isotopes is correct?

options.text: They are all much the same, since every unstable nucleus decays at a similar rate.
options.rationale: Classroom examples all use convenient half-lives, so students never see the extremes and assume a narrow band.

options.text: They all lie between a few seconds and a few days, for any isotope at all.
options.rationale: This is the range met in decay-curve practice questions, so it is taken to be the range that exists in nature.

options.text: They change with the temperature and the pressure a sample is kept at.
options.rationale: Students transfer the idea that rates of change depend on conditions from chemical reactions to nuclear decay.

options.text: They cover a very wide range, from fractions of a second to billions of years.
options.rationale: The specification states that radioactive isotopes have a very wide range of half-life values.

mcqs.stem: A radioactive isotope with a half-life of many thousands of years is spilled onto open ground. Why is such a long half-life a particular hazard here?

options.text: The ground stays radioactive for a very long time after the spill.
options.rationale: A long half-life means the activity falls only very slowly, so the contamination remains a hazard for generations.

options.text: Its activity is enormous, so it emits a great deal of radiation now.
options.rationale: Long is read as more radioactive, whereas a long half-life in fact means comparatively few decays each second.

options.text: Isotopes with a long half-life always emit alpha, the worst kind of all.
options.rationale: Half-life and type of emission are independent, but students often bundle every hazardous property together.

options.text: It decays so fast that it spreads over the whole area at once.
options.rationale: Half-life is confused with the speed at which material moves, and a long half-life with rapid decay.

mcqs.stem: A source with a half-life of a few minutes is spilled in a school laboratory. Why is it a serious hazard at once but much less of one an hour later?

options.text: The nuclei all stop decaying once one half-life has gone by.
options.rationale: Half-life is taken as the lifetime of the sample, so decay is assumed to end rather than to continue at a falling rate.

options.text: Its activity is high at first and then falls away fast.
options.rationale: A short half-life means very many decays each second at the start, and that rate halves every few minutes, so the hazard is immediate but brief.

options.text: A short half-life means it gives out no radiation at all.
options.rationale: Students learn that short-lived sources are chosen to protect patients and conclude that short half-life means harmless.

options.text: Its radiation changes from gamma into harmless alpha rays.
options.rationale: The type of emission is imagined to soften with time, and alpha is wrongly thought of as the mildest radiation.

mcqs.stem: A tracer is injected so that a doctor can watch how a patient's kidneys are working. Which property makes an isotope suitable for this use?

options.text: It emits alpha radiation, which is easily detected through the skin.
options.rationale: Strongly ionising is equated with easily detected, without checking whether the radiation can leave the body at all.

options.text: It has a half-life of many years, so the scan could be repeated later.
options.rationale: Convenience for the hospital is weighed instead of the dose to the patient, who would stay radioactive for years.

options.text: It emits radiation intense enough to destroy the tissue it reaches.
options.rationale: The two medical uses are merged, so the destructive property wanted in therapy is applied to a diagnostic tracer.

options.text: It emits gamma radiation, which leaves the body and is detected outside.
options.rationale: Gamma radiation is penetrating and weakly ionising, so it passes out to a detector while depositing comparatively little energy in the patient.

mcqs.stem: How are nuclear radiations used to control or destroy a tumour lying deep inside the body?

options.text: A high dose of gamma radiation is aimed at the tumour from outside.
options.rationale: External beam radiotherapy uses a high dose of penetrating gamma radiation directed at the tumour, often rotated around the patient.

options.text: A weak alpha source is swallowed and travels to the tumour site itself.
options.rationale: Alpha is assumed to travel wherever it is needed, when in fact skin or paper stops it and it penetrates less than a millimetre of tissue.

options.text: A tracer is injected and its gamma rays then shrink the tumour.
options.rationale: The diagnostic use is confused with the therapeutic one, so a small tracer dose is imagined to be a treatment.

options.text: The tumour is cooled by radiation until its cells stop dividing.
options.rationale: Radiation is thought to act by changing temperature rather than by ionising and damaging the cells it passes through.

mcqs.stem: A gamma-emitting tracer with a half-life of about six hours is chosen instead of one with a half-life of several years. Evaluate this choice.

options.text: Poor: a source that decays this quickly cannot give out enough radiation to be detected.
options.rationale: Short half-life is read as weak, when it in fact means a high activity for the short period that the scan needs.

options.text: Good: the activity falls quickly, so the patient's dose after the scan stays small.
options.rationale: A half-life of hours gives ample activity for imaging and then decays away, limiting the dose received once the scan is over.

options.text: It makes no difference: the tracer leaves the body within a day whatever its half-life.
options.rationale: Excretion is assumed to solve the problem entirely, so the decay rate is treated as irrelevant to the dose.

options.text: Poor: a longer-lived tracer would let the doctors scan the same organ again later.
options.rationale: Only the convenience to the hospital is weighed, ignoring the years of unnecessary exposure it would give the patient.

mcqs.stem: A scan using a radioactive tracer gives a patient a dose of about 6 mSv. The average annual dose from background radiation is about 2.7 mSv. The patient refuses the scan, saying that any nuclear radiation is too dangerous. Which is the best evaluation of that decision?

options.text: The dose is close to one year of background radiation, so there is no risk.
options.rationale: Over-correcting the fear into zero risk is as poor an evaluation as refusing outright, and the data do not support it.

options.text: Refusing is right, because man-made radiation harms the body more than background.
options.rationale: Radiation from a man-made source is assumed to be different in kind, when the same dose carries the same risk.

options.text: The small added risk should be weighed against the benefit of a diagnosis.
options.rationale: Evaluating a perceived risk against given data means comparing a dose of a few millisieverts with the consequences of leaving an illness undiagnosed.

options.text: Refusing is right, since a dose above background is certain to cause a cancer.
options.rationale: Any excess dose is treated as a guaranteed consequence rather than as a small increase in probability.

mcqs.stem: A gamma beam rotated around a patient destroys a deep tumour, but it also passes through healthy tissue. Evaluate this treatment.

options.text: Justified: the tumour is destroyed and the dose to healthy tissue is limited.
options.rationale: Rotating the beam spreads the dose to healthy tissue over a large volume while the tumour stays in the path, so the benefit outweighs the side effects.

options.text: Ideal: careful aiming means that only the tumour receives any radiation.
options.rationale: Targeting is read as perfect, but the beam must pass through healthy tissue on its way in, which is why side effects occur.

options.text: Unjustified: no dose of nuclear radiation to a patient is acceptable.
options.rationale: A blanket refusal ignores the consequence of leaving the tumour untreated, which is far more dangerous than the dose.

options.text: Ineffective: gamma is too weakly ionising to damage a deep tumour.
options.rationale: Weakly ionising is confused with harmless; a therapy beam delivers a very high dose, so enough ionisation reaches the tumour to kill its cells.
